lead: On the solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul the Church honours the two apostles who gave their lives in Rome and whom she calls her pillars. The first reading tells how the Lord rescued Peter from Herod’s prison while the church prayed for him. In the second, Paul, near the end, says, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith,” and trusts that the Lord will rescue him for his heavenly kingdom. In the Gospel Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and Jesus answers, “you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.”

Psalm 34 joins the readings: “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them.” Both apostles were rescued many times, and in the end both were delivered through martyrdom into the kingdom. The Vigil Mass has its own readings (Acts 3:1–10; Galatians 1:11–20; John 21:15–19).

r.h: The Lord has sent his angel and rescued me
set: King Herod here is Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea from about 41 to 44 AD. He killed James, the brother of John, the first of the Twelve to be martyred, and then arrested Peter at the time of the Passover. Luke tells the story so that it recalls the first Passover: a night of deliverance, an angel of the Lord, a command to rise quickly with belt and sandals.

Luke writes that Herod saw that the killing of James “pleased the Jews”. In Acts this refers to the leaders and those in Jerusalem who at that moment opposed the apostles, not to the Jewish people as a whole. Peter, James and the whole Jerusalem church were themselves Jews, and Luke records that many thousands of Jews believed (Acts 21:20).
str: vv. 1–4: Herod kills James and imprisons Peter during the feast of Unleavened Bread.
v. 5: Peter is kept in prison; the church prays fervently for him.
vv. 6–7: the night before his trial, an angel wakes Peter; the chains fall off.
vv. 8–10: belt, sandals, cloak; through the guards and the iron gate.
v. 11: Peter comes to himself: “Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me.”
kw: Stretched out, earnestly, without stopping. A related word describes Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). The whole church is at prayer while Peter sleeps.
The heavenly messenger who acts for God. The angel of the Lord also opened the prison doors for the apostles earlier (5:19).
Delivered, snatched out. The same verb is used by Stephen of God rescuing Joseph and Israel in Egypt (7:10, 34). Peter’s night is a small exodus.
vv: He had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword.
The first apostle to die for Christ. Jesus had told James and John that they would drink his cup (Mark 10:39).
While Peter was kept in prison, the church prayed fervently to God for him.
Two powers face each other: the prison of the king and the prayer of the church. Luke shows which one is stronger.
Peter, bound with two chains, was sleeping between two soldiers,
He sleeps on the night before his trial. Peter, who once slept in Gethsemane from weakness, now sleeps in peace, trusting God.
Fasten your belt and put on your sandals.
The words recall the Passover command: “your loins girded, your sandals on your feet” (Exodus 12:11). It happens during the same feast.
Now I am sure that the Lord has sent his angel and rescued me
Only when he stands in the street does Peter understand. Faith often recognises God’s action afterwards.
ch: The Church sees in this reading the power of prayer for the Pope and the bishops. The Catechism teaches that the Roman Pontiff, as Peter’s successor, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity both of the bishops and of the whole company of the faithful (CCC 882, quoting Lumen Gentium 23). In every Mass the Church names the Pope and the bishop of the diocese in the Eucharistic Prayer, praying for them as the Jerusalem church prayed for Peter. The angel’s rescue does not mean that Peter will never suffer. He will be rescued many times, and in the end will give his life, as Jesus foretold (John 21:18–19).

set: The Second Letter to Timothy presents Paul as a prisoner in Rome, near the end of his life, writing to his beloved disciple. It is one of the three Pastoral Letters. Many scholars think these letters were written by a disciple of Paul in his name after his death; others hold that Paul wrote them himself. The Church receives them as inspired Scripture, the voice of Paul to the Church.
Today’s verses are Paul’s farewell. He looks back on his life, and forward to the judgment, and remembers how the Lord stood by him when everyone else deserted him at his first defence (4:16).
str: v. 6: I am already being poured out as a libation; the time of my departure has come.
v. 7: the good fight, the race, the faith kept.
v. 8: the crown of righteousness, for me and for all who have longed for his appearing.
vv. 17–18: the Lord stood by me and gave me strength; he will rescue me for his heavenly kingdom. Glory to him.
kw: to be poured out as a libation
In ancient sacrifices wine or oil was poured out on the altar. Paul sees his coming death as an offering poured out to God (compare Philippians 2:17).
A word used for loosing a ship from its moorings or striking a tent. Death is a setting out, not an end.
The wreath given to the winner in the games. Paul has finished the race; the Lord, the just judge, will give the crown.
vv: As for me, I am already being poured out as a libation,
Paul’s life has been given to God day by day. His martyrdom will be the last drop of the offering.
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
Three pictures: the athlete in the contest, the runner at the finishing line, and the steward who has kept safe what was entrusted to him. It is not pride, but thanksgiving for grace.
and not only to me but also to all who have longed for his appearing.
The crown is not only for apostles. It is promised to every believer who loves the Lord’s coming.
But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength,
When others left him, the Lord did not. Paul’s whole mission depended on that strength, so that “all the Gentiles might hear”.
To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
Paul ends with praise. Even in chains, the last word belongs to God.
ch: From the earliest times the Church has honoured Peter and Paul together. St Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth about the year 96, recalled the two great apostles who suffered in his own day; St Irenaeus spoke of the Church of Rome as founded and organised by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul (Against Heresies 3.3.2). The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). In today’s Preface the Church praises God that Peter was foremost in confessing the faith and Paul its outstanding preacher, and that both, by different ways, gathered together the one family of Christ.

r.h: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church
set: Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, near the sources of the Jordan, in the territory of Herod’s son Philip. It was a place of pagan shrines, built against a great rock face. There, far from Jerusalem, Jesus asks his disciples who he is.
Mark and Luke tell Peter’s confession too, but only Matthew gives Jesus’ answer to Peter with the blessing, the new name, the promise of the Church and the keys.
str: vv. 13–14: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah, a prophet.
vv. 15–16: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter: “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”
v. 17: Blessed are you; my Father revealed this to you.
v. 18: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church; the gates of Hades will not prevail.
v. 19: the keys of the kingdom; binding and loosing.
kw: In Greek the name Peter (Petros) and the word rock (petra) are nearly the same. In Aramaic, which Jesus spoke, the word is the same, Kēpāʾ; that is why Paul often calls him Cephas (1 Corinthians 15:5; Galatians 2:9).
The assembly called together. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew word for the assembly of Israel. Jesus speaks of “my church”, the people he gathers.

Isaiah 22:22 tells how the key of the house of David was given to Eliakim, the steward of the king’s palace: “he shall open, and no one shall shut.” The keys mean authority over the house in the name of the king.
vv: But who do you say that I am?
The question is addressed to every generation. Opinions about Jesus are not enough; he asks for a personal answer.
You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.
Peter speaks for all the Twelve. The confession joins the hope of Israel, the Messiah, with the deepest truth of Jesus, the Son of God.
For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven.
Faith is a gift from the Father, not a human discovery. The Catechism uses this verse to teach that faith is a grace (CCC 153).
you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
Simon receives a new name that is a mission. The Church is Christ’s (“my church”), built by him on Peter. The powers of death will not overcome it.
whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.

In Jewish teaching, to bind and loose meant to forbid and permit, and also to exclude from the community and to receive back. What Peter does in Christ’s name, heaven confirms. The same power is later given to the apostles together (18:18).
ch: The Catechism teaches that Peter’s confession of Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, was the Father’s gift, and that on the rock of this faith confessed by St Peter Christ built his Church (CCC 424, 442). It teaches that Jesus entrusted a specific authority to Peter: the power of the keys designates authority to govern the house of God, which is the Church (CCC 553), and that the Lord made Simon alone the rock of his Church, while the office of binding and loosing was also given to the college of apostles united to its head (CCC 881). The Second Vatican Council teaches the same in Lumen Gentium 18 and 22. Peter’s authority comes from Christ, and it is a service of unity.

qa: Is the rock Peter himself or Peter’s faith?

Both, and the two are not opposed. Some Fathers emphasised Peter’s faith, others Peter himself. The Catechism says Christ built his Church “on the rock of this faith confessed by St Peter” (CCC 424), and also that the Lord “made Simon alone… the rock of his Church” (CCC 881). The rock is Peter the believer, confessing the faith given by the Father, and his successors who keep that faith for the whole Church.
Why are Peter and Paul celebrated on the same day?

Because tradition holds that both gave their lives in Rome under Nero, Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the sword, and the Church of Rome has kept their memory together since ancient times. A Roman calendar of the fourth century already lists 29 June. The two were very different, the fisherman from Galilee and the learned Pharisee from Tarsus, and they even disagreed openly once (Galatians 2:11–14), but they were united in Christ and in martyrdom.
What does this feast mean for Christians who do not accept the Pope’s authority?

Orthodox and many other Christians also honour Peter and Paul and keep this feast. The Catholic Church holds that Christ gave Peter and his successors a ministry of unity. St John Paul II, aware that the papacy has also been a difficulty for other Christians, invited them to help find a way of exercising this ministry that all could recognise (Ut Unum Sint 95). On this feast Catholics pray for the Pope and for the unity of all who believe in Christ.
rite: In the Latin Church today is a solemnity. In Rome the Holy Father blesses the pallia, the woollen bands worn by metropolitan archbishops as a sign of their communion with the Successor of Peter, for the archbishops appointed in the past year. Peter’s Pence, the offering of the faithful for the Pope’s works of charity, is traditionally linked with this day. Tomorrow the Church remembers the first martyrs of Rome, who died under Nero in the same persecution. The bones honoured as St Peter’s lie beneath the high altar of St Peter’s Basilica, and St Paul’s tomb is venerated in the basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls.
study: Jesus asks, “But who do you say that I am?” How would I answer in my own words, today?
The church prayed fervently for Peter in prison. Do I pray regularly for the Pope and my bishop? How could my family make this a habit?
Paul says, “I have kept the faith.” What have I received in faith that I must hand on to my children or to others?
Peter and Paul were very different men. What can our parish learn from them about unity among people who are not alike?
